paras: The lynching of John Jeffress took place on August 25, 1920, near Graham, North Carolina, when a mob took the Black prisoner from Sheriff C. D. Story and his deputies on the way to court and shot him outside town. He had been arrested that morning, charged with attacking a young white girl, and a grand jury had already indicted him. The killing came a month after machine gunners had turned back a mob at the same jail, and it led to calls for the sheriff's removal.

On the night of July 19, Durham machine gunners guarding the Alamance county jail had fought a masked mob, and James Ray was killed. By late August the Guardsmen had been withdrawn and Superior Court was in session at Graham under Judge Allen.

According to the Durham AP account, at about 10 that morning Jeffress grabbed Mary Rudd, daughter of A. L. Rudd, near her home close to Elon College and allegedly attempted criminal assault. Other versions said the mother's cries frightened him away before the child was harmed, and gave her age as four, six, seven or eight. A posse found Jeffress hiding in honeysuckle near the Graham railroad station and jailed him; the sheriff said he admitted the crime.

It was court week, and several hundred people had gathered around the jail and courthouse. At 3 o'clock, as officers took Jeffress toward the courthouse a block away, a mob surrounded them at the spot where Ray had died, seized him and drove off in an automobile. The sheriff said no shot was fired, that resistance would have been folly against 25 to 50 determined men, and that he recognized no one.

The Burlington News reported that the men took him to the first woods on the Billemont road, about two miles from Graham, threw him out and shot him. A United Press dispatch said the coroner found twenty bullet holes in the body. Within twenty minutes, by that account, a thousand people had viewed the body, and visitors, 'many ladies' among them, came all afternoon.

That night Sheriff Story said he had not visited the scene and did not know whether a coroner's inquest had been held. At the close of the term, the grand jury found that Jeffress had been taken by 'unknown persons' and shot, and that the officers had done all they could to protect him.

The Raleigh Times demanded the sheriff's removal; it accepted Graham's word that the lynchers were outsiders who came in a big automobile but doubted that they came from outside Alamance County. C. B. Riddle, editor of the Christian Sun at Burlington, answered that the Times editor had not been there to see it, and a deputy described the mob as 'foreigners' and 'giants'.

White newspapers across the country carried AP versions from Graham and Durham and a UP brief from Burlington on August 26. Headlines such as 'Negro Is Lynched for Usual Crime' and 'Admits Crime and Pays Penalty at Hands of a Small Mob' presented the charge and the sheriff's report of a confession as settled. The New York Sun kept the charge as an accusation, and the Hickory Daily Record's editorial page faulted the sheriff and his deputies for cutting 'a pretty sorry figure'.

The Raleigh Independent reprinted the Raleigh Times exchange and wrote in its own editorial that 'Graham's lust for blood is satisfied'. The Richmond Planet and Metropolis Weekly Gazette reprinted AP texts in September. The Dallas Express called the accusation a 'frivolous charge' giving the mob revenge for July, and the Chicago Whip labeled a white editorial praising the lynchers' 'well carried out plan' 'The Week's Worst Editorial'.

The sheriff's account, repeated by the AP and accepted by the grand jury, described a sudden seizure by a crowd the officers could not resist. The Chicago Whip reported instead that the sheriff turned his prisoner over to a mob of 150 and that the 'assault' was Jeffress speaking to the girl; the Dallas Express said the sheriff knew the mob's plans. Estimates of the mob ranged from the UP's 'eight masked men' to the sheriff's unmasked 25 to 50.

accounts.label: Sheriff's account (AP Durham wire)
accounts.gist: A mob of 25 to 50 surged around the sheriff and six assistants a block from the courthouse, seized the prisoner in an instant and drove off; no shot was fired and resistance would have been folly. The sheriff said Jeffress had admitted the crime.

accounts.label: AP Graham dispatch
accounts.gist: A mob of about fifty overpowered the sheriff and six deputies during a transfer for a preliminary hearing and shot Jeffress a mile and a half outside Graham; the mother's cries had frightened him away before the child was harmed.

accounts.label: UP Burlington dispatch
accounts.gist: Eight masked men overpowered the sheriff and seven deputies as the 18-year-old was taken to court after a true bill; he was said to have confessed, and the coroner found twenty bullet holes.

accounts.label: Burlington News (quoted by the Raleigh Times)
accounts.gist: The car reached the first woods on the Billemont road in about three minutes; the men threw him out and shot him without using the rope they carried, and a thousand people viewed the body within twenty minutes.

accounts.label: Alamance grand jury
accounts.gist: Found Jeffers was taken from the officers by unknown persons and shot, and that the sheriff and officers had done all they could to protect him.

accounts.label: Chicago Whip correspondent
accounts.gist: The sheriff and six deputies turned the prisoner over to a mob of 150 at a lonely spot; the alleged assault consisted of his speaking to the girl as he passed her house.

accounts.label: Dallas Express
accounts.gist: The charge was frivolous and a pretext for revenge after the failed July attack on the jail; the sheriff knew of the mob's plans and said at least 160 more men nearby sympathized with it.

framing.detail: AP stories ran under headlines such as 'Negro Is Lynched for Usual Crime' and 'Admits Crime and Pays Penalty at Hands of a Small Mob', resting the confession on the sheriff's word.
The New York Sun's 'Mob Riddles Negro Accused of Attack' kept the charge as an accusation and noted the child was not harmed.
The Hickory Daily Record's editorial page mocked the sheriff and his seven deputies for cutting 'a pretty sorry figure' without condemning the lynching itself.

The Raleigh Independent reprinted the Raleigh Times editorial demanding Sheriff Story's removal, which also called Jeffress 'the brute' and assumed his guilt, along with a Burlington editor's defense of the town.
The Raleigh Independent's own editorial said Graham 'had to have its lynching' and ended with 'Graham's lust for blood is satisfied'.

The Chicago Whip said the assault was only a greeting and that the sheriff handed over his prisoner to be executed by the 'laws of the South', and named a white editorial praising the lynchers' plan 'The Week's Worst Editorial'.
The Dallas Express headlined a 'Frivolous Charge Produced to Give Mob Chance to Get Revenge For Former Failure'.
The Richmond Planet and Metropolis Weekly Gazette reprinted AP texts; the Gazette's headline stressed that the mother had frightened the man away before the child was harmed.

record_check.dossier: Accused of an attempted attack on a young white girl (Mary Rudd), said to have been unharmed; the Chicago Whip said he only spoke to her.
The pursuit was by a lawful posse before the arrest; the mob's acts were seizure from officers, abduction by automobile, shooting and killing.
Unknown; the grand jury found 'unknown persons'; mob size given variously from eight to 150.
White coverage ran Aug. 26-27 in at least 15 papers; Black papers (Raleigh Independent, Richmond Planet, Chicago Whip, Metropolis Weekly Gazette, Dallas Express) covered it Sept. 4-11.
John Jeffress, also printed Jeffries, Jefferies and Jeffers; UP gave his age as 18.
